name: Tichel

lead: A tichel (Hebrew: mitpachat) is a cloth headscarf worn by many married Orthodox Jewish women to cover their hair in line with Jewish law and custom. For wearers it is both a religious garment and a styling choice: it frames the face, and fabric, colour and tying style can be changed to suit an outfit or occasion.

It is one of several covering options, alongside wigs (sheitels), snoods, hats and berets. Some Sephardi and National Religious women prefer scarves because their rabbis consider wigs insufficiently modest. Some non-Orthodox women have also adopted head coverings in recent decades.

paras: The scarf is wrapped and tied around the head in a range of styles, from a plain wrap to elaborate versions using several fabrics. A padded cap, sometimes called a shaper, volumizer or bobo, is sometimes worn underneath to give a fuller shape. Most authorities expect all or most of the hair to be covered.
There are no health risks specific to a scarf. Wearing it for long periods can leave tight styling pressure on the hairline, and some wearers combine it with other coverings for comfort in heat.

lead: A tichel is a headscarf worn to cover a married woman's hair. Tichel is Yiddish, a diminutive of the word for cloth; the Hebrew term is mitpachat.[1]

For people interested in looks, it is a hair-covering accessory in which fabric, colour, tying style and the padded underlayer can all be varied, and it sits alongside wigs, snoods and hats as a way of dressing the head.[1]

Its main purpose is religious. Married Orthodox women are expected to cover their hair in front of men who are not close relatives, and the covering also signals married status and community identification.[1] On the T Nation forum, a poster describing Orthodox practice named wigs, the tichel and hats as the usual options.[2]
infobox: Married Orthodox Jewish women; some others

paras: A tichel can be a plain square or rectangle of any fabric, or an elaborate wrap using several fabrics and tying methods; how it is tied tends to track how casually the wearer is dressed.[1] A padded cap worn underneath creates a fuller shape.[1]
Most authorities require most or all hair to be covered, though some allow a small amount to show and differ on how much.[1]

Reasons given include dignity, since uncovering the head was historically humiliating; modesty; signalling married status; and awe before God, comparable to the kippah for men.[1] Today it also expresses identification with a religious community, and some non-Orthodox women wear one as a sign of devotion, ethnic identity or reclaimed modest dress.[1]

The Mishnah lists appearing in public with uncovered hair among grounds for divorce, described as a breach of Jewish custom.[1] The twelfth-century commentator Abraham ibn Ezra wrote that Israelite women wore head cloths like those of Muslim women of his day, and nineteenth-century photographs show Jewish women in headscarves in Tunisia and Poland.[1]
